timeline/character/description: Author of the Masnavi, one of the greatest poets of the Persian language, and the source of the Mevlevi order
timeline/stages/0/summary: At twelve he left Samarkand with his family and spent six years walking west. In a spice shop in Nishapur the boy heard a story about thirty birds; in a small Anatolian town the family finally stopped — and in a single year he married and buried his mother.
timeline/stages/0/events/0/summary: His father takes the household out of Samarkand. Later writers say it was to escape the Mongols — but when they left, the Mongols had not yet come.
timeline/stages/0/events/0/poemAnchor/la: Cut from the reed bed (paid off in 1258)
timeline/stages/0/events/1/summary: The old poet Attar takes one look at the boy and tells him a story: thirty birds fly over seven valleys to find their king, and at the end they see themselves in the surface of a lake.
timeline/stages/0/events/2/name: A Wedding and a Funeral in Larende
timeline/stages/0/events/2/state: Joy and grief in one year
timeline/stages/0/events/2/summary: After six years on the road the family stops in a small Anatolian town. Rumi marries at eighteen; that same year his mother is buried here.
timeline/stages/1/summary: The Seljuk sultan invites the family to his capital. After his father's death the twenty-four-year-old Rumi takes over the teaching chair; then his own teacher sends him to Syria to read to the end of the books, and afterwards shuts him away for forty days, three times over.
timeline/stages/1/events/0/summary: His father dies. At twenty-four Rumi stands at the lectern for the first time, with his father's old students sitting below. When it is over, Burhan al-Din says one sentence to him.
timeline/stages/1/events/1/summary: Years of law and scripture in Aleppo and Damascus, then a full house of students back in Konya. And then his teacher asks him to shut himself away for forty days — three times — and do nothing at all.
timeline/stages/2/summary: In the autumn of 1244 a stranger stops him in the street and asks a question no book can answer. Over the next three years Rumi writes a thousand poems; then the man vanishes, and no one ever sees him again.
timeline/stages/2/events/0/summary: The books go into the pool and there is time to save only one. In the street a man in a black felt cap asks: 「And you yourself — what do you know?」 This time every answer is refused.
timeline/stages/2/events/0/poemAnchor/la: The closing couplet carries the name of Shams
timeline/stages/2/events/1/summary: Shams disappears a second time. Rumi carries a lamp through the Damascus bazaar, following one lead after another, and every one comes to nothing. Where did he go? The sources have no answer.
timeline/stages/3/summary: He gets back on his feet inside the hammer-beat of an illiterate goldsmith. In 1258 the world is collapsing and he begins dictating a long poem — and goes on dictating it for fifteen years. The last night of all, he called a wedding.
timeline/stages/3/events/0/state: Standing up again inside a rhythm
timeline/stages/3/events/0/summary: After losing Shams, Rumi finds a companion again in a goldsmith who cannot read. The story goes that he passed the shop, heard the hammering, and began to turn in the street.
timeline/stages/3/events/1/summary: The year the Mongols take Baghdad, his disciple Husam al-Din picks up pen and paper and Rumi begins to speak. The Masnavi nests a hundred parables inside one another, and every one of them says: you thought A — it is B.
timeline/stages/3/events/1/poemAnchor/la: Listen to this reed — it is telling of separation
timeline/stages/3/events/2/summary: 「Do not weep. This is my wedding.」 On the day of the funeral the procession held Muslims, and Christians, and Jews. Seven hundred years later people still call that night the Wedding Night.
events/1219_balkh/phases/0/transitionTex:
Konya, 1291.
My name is Sultan Walad. I am writing the life of my father — the book came to be called the Ebtedâ-nâme, the Book of Beginnings.
events/1219_balkh/phases/0/announcement/:
「The year my father turned twelve, the household left Samarkand. Later people say it was to escape the Mongols.
But when my grandfather set out, the Mongols had not yet come.
— Why did he go?」
events/1219_balkh/phases/1/situation: Samarkand. Twelve-year-old Rumi has heard that the family is leaving — for Mecca, and perhaps for good. The grown-ups will not tell a child why. Behind the mud wall of the bazaar, people are talking.
events/1219_balkh/phases/1/instruction: Put your ear to the wall and slide it along. The closer you are to someone, the clearer they get.
events/1219_balkh/phases/1/voices/0/text: 「Samarkand melons — even the Caliph in Baghdad sends for them!」
events/1219_balkh/phases/1/voices/0/why: Samarkand is rich — that explains why leaving is hard, not why they are leaving.
events/1219_balkh/phases/1/voices/1/text: 「Something happened at Otrar — a caravan sent by the Mongol khan, every man of it killed. The khan will not let that lie.」
events/1219_balkh/phases/1/voices/1/why: The danger outside: Khwarazm killed a Mongol caravan (1218) and war is coming.
events/1219_balkh/phases/1/voices/2/text: 「Your father says we are going to Mecca on pilgrimage. Bring only what matters most.」
events/1219_balkh/phases/1/voices/2/why: Pilgrimage is the reason given in public — it does not explain why they must go at all, taking the whole household and the library with them.
events/1219_balkh/phases/1/voices/3/text: 「Every time Baha al-Din preaches he is cursing the scholars at court. The palace has hated him for years.」
events/1219_balkh/phases/1/voices/3/why: The trouble inside: he is badly at odds with the court and its scholars.
events/1219_balkh/phases/1/voices/4/text: 「Silk has doubled this year, and I still cannot get a bolt of it.」
events/1219_balkh/phases/1/voices/4/why: True, and perhaps connected to the unrest — but it is about business, and it cannot explain why this one family is leaving.
events/1219_balkh/phases/1/voices/5/text: 「There was once a king, and he had forty camels…」
events/1219_balkh/phases/1/claim: Baha al-Din took his household out of Samarkand for more than one reason.
events/1219_balkh/phases/1/reveal:
One reason outside: the Mongols are coming. One reason inside: he has fallen out with the court.
Later biographies usually give only the first — “to escape the Mongols.” But when the family left, the Mongol army was still years away from Samarkand. One reason alone cannot explain why they went so early.
events/1219_balkh/phases/1/consequence: Scholars disagree about the exact year of departure (roughly 1212–1219). What is certain is what came after: Samarkand, Bukhara and Balkh all fell in the Mongol campaign. Baha al-Din's family never returned to Khorasan.
events/1219_balkh/phases/2/prompt: The caravan leaves at first light. You may take three things.
events/1219_balkh/phases/2/verdict:
Samarkand — fallen
Bukhara — fallen
Balkh — fallen
events/1219_balkh/phases/2/line: This family never returned to Khorasan.
events/1219_balkh/phases/3/travelNarrati: The caravan goes west. This is the trunk of the Silk Road, one oasis city after another — and not one of them knows how many years it has left.
events/1219_balkh/phases/3/instruction: Click each stop along the route.
events/1219_balkh/phases/3/waypoints/0/d: 「Look back once. Remember how it is now.」
events/1219_balkh/phases/3/waypoints/1/d: Bukhara, one of the oldest cities of learning in Central Asia. Next year it will be burned.
events/1219_balkh/phases/3/waypoints/2/d: The driest stretch of the desert. Here the waterskins decide how fast the family can travel.
(If the waterskins were left behind — your mother gives you her share.)
events/1219_balkh/phases/3/waypoints/3/d: 「We rest here a few days. There is an old man in the city who sells spices. I want to take you to meet him.」
events/1220_nishapur/phases/0/title: Nishapur · the spice and medicine shop
events/1220_nishapur/phases/0/narrative:
The caravan halts at Nishapur. Your father takes you into a shop — the walls are a grid of little drawers of herbs and spices, a brass balance, bottles of rose water.
The name “Attar” means exactly that: the man who sells spices and medicines.
events/1220_nishapur/phases/0/instructio: Three people in the shop. Talk to all of them.
events/1220_nishapur/phases/0/npcs/0/dia: 「What does the gentleman need? Frankincense, myrrh, rose water — we have all of it.」
「The master? He weighs medicine by day and writes at night. None of us can make sense of what he writes.」
events/1220_nishapur/phases/0/npcs/1/dia: 「There is no one in Khorasan who has not read this old man's poems.」
events/1220_nishapur/phases/0/npcs/2/dia: 「By day I weigh medicine. At night I write poems.」
「Medicine treats what is wrong with the body. Poems treat something else.」
「Sit down, child. I will tell you a story — about a flock of birds who went looking for their king.」
events/1220_nishapur/phases/1/legend: Attar, The Conference of the Birds · retold for this work
events/1220_nishapur/phases/1/situation: In the spice shop in Nishapur, the old poet Attar tells thirteen-year-old Rumi a story: every bird in the world sets out to find its king, the Simurgh. The hoopoe leads the way.
events/1220_nishapur/phases/1/valleys/0/: Put down everything you carry, or you cannot enter.
「The rose withers in a season — and it is laughing at you even now.」
Thread the gaps between the rock pillars
events/1220_nishapur/phases/1/valleys/1/: Love is a fire. It does not argue.
「All I want is the water of eternal life.」
「You want to live forever, and will not risk anything once to get it.」
The wall of fire cannot be dodged — hold to dash straight through
events/1220_nishapur/phases/1/valleys/2/: No two birds see the same road.
「I only want to get back to the garden of paradise.」
「The garden is one corner of the house. It is not the house.」
Gather the scattered light — you will need it in the last valley
events/1220_nishapur/phases/1/valleys/3/: 「You have washed all your life and never once asked what you were washing off.」
Keep the flock off the gold and the jewels
events/1220_nishapur/phases/1/valleys/4/: 「I am doing very well on the king's wrist.」
「The king's wrist can also throw you down.」
Wind coming — hold to dash and pull the flock in tight
events/1220_nishapur/phases/1/valleys/5/: You no longer know what you know.
「I have a treasure to guard among the ruins.」
「You guard the treasure, and the treasure keeps you shut in the ruins.」
Up and down have swapped… and the stones are floating
events/1220_nishapur/phases/1/valleys/6/: 「I am too small. I cannot fly any further.」
「Every bird on this road is afraid. Fear is not a reason to turn back.」
events/1220_nishapur/phases/1/question: Thirty birds finally reach the palace of the Simurgh. Where is the king they came to find?
events/1220_nishapur/phases/1/options/0/: Inside the palace — a golden bird larger than a mountain
events/1220_nishapur/phases/1/options/1/: The hoopoe who led them is the Simurgh
events/1220_nishapur/phases/1/options/2/: On the surface of the lake: thirty reflections, together making one great bird
events/1220_nishapur/phases/1/options/3/: The palace is empty. There is no Simurgh at all
events/1220_nishapur/phases/1/reveal:
In Persian, “Simurgh” (sī murgh) taken apart reads “thirty birds.”
The king they came to find is the ones who finished the flight.
events/1220_nishapur/phases/1/consequenc:
In Attar's poem the birds who drop out are not only the ones with excuses — others die of thirst, drown, burn, are eaten. Tens of thousands set out; thirty arrive.
Twenty-four years from now, Rumi will meet a man in Konya who asks him a question — and you will think of this lake again.
events/1220_nishapur/phases/2/transition: As they are leaving, the old man takes one of his own books down from the shelf and puts it into the boy's hands.
events/1220_nishapur/phases/2/announceme: Attar says to Baha al-Din: 「This child will one day set a fire in the world.」
events/1220_nishapur/phases/2/narrative:
Walad: 「My father never once mentioned this to me. It was written down later.
You are free not to believe it — but look: the fire did come.」

The following year the Mongol army took Nishapur and put the city to the sword. Attar, the story goes, died in the massacre.
events/1225_larende/title: A Wedding and a Funeral in Larende
events/1225_larende/phases/0/travelNarra:
The family goes south-west as far as Mecca, then turns north-west. Six or seven years of walking and stopping.
(The sources disagree on the details of the route; only the mainstream account is used here.)
events/1225_larende/phases/0/instruction: Click each stop along the route.
events/1225_larende/phases/0/waypoints/0: The Caliph's capital, one of the largest cities on earth at the time. Thirty-three years from now it will be burned to the ground.
events/1225_larende/phases/0/waypoints/1: 「We said we were coming on pilgrimage. Here we are.」
events/1225_larende/phases/0/waypoints/2: The city with more scholars than any other. Eight years from now Rumi will come back here alone, to study.
events/1225_larende/phases/0/waypoints/3: Seljuk country. The language has changed, and so has the food.
events/1225_larende/phases/0/waypoints/4: 「Let it be here. I cannot walk any further.」
events/1225_larende/phases/1/narrative: A small town in Anatolia. A stone courtyard, a vine trellis, coloured cloths hung under the arcade — there is a wedding in the house.
events/1225_larende/phases/1/instruction: Three people in the courtyard. Talk to all of them.
events/1225_larende/phases/1/npcs/0/dial: 「My father and your father were friends back in Samarkand.」
「Our two households lost each other on the same road, and found each other again on it.」
events/1225_larende/phases/1/npcs/1/dial: 「It took us six years to walk from Samarkand to here.」
「You grew up on that road. I grew old on it.」
events/1225_larende/phases/1/npcs/2/dial: 「The pen is on the desk. So is the paper.」
events/1225_larende/phases/2/situation: A blank marriage contract lies open on the low desk. A reed pen, an inkwell, a sand shaker, and one red candle beside them.
events/1225_larende/phases/2/question: Writing a contract in Persian — which side does the pen start from?
events/1225_larende/phases/2/options/0/t: Left to right, the way Chinese runs across a page
events/1225_larende/phases/2/options/2/t: Top to bottom, column by column
events/1225_larende/phases/2/sameNote: Right. Then you already know that this family's books open at what looks to us like the last page.
events/1225_larende/phases/2/reveal:
Persian is written in the Arabic script, right to left.
The books open at what looks to us like the last page.
events/1225_larende/phases/2/consequence: Rumi wrote poetry in this script all his life. The Masnavi alone runs to some twenty-five thousand couplets, every one of them written right to left.
events/1225_larende/phases/3/instruction: Click the picture and open it one panel at a time.
events/1225_larende/phases/3/panels/0/di: The wedding. Musicians playing under the arcade, the couple with their heads lowered.
events/1225_larende/phases/3/panels/1/di: Not long after, his mother fell ill.
events/1225_larende/phases/3/panels/2/di: The household put on plain clothes.
events/1225_larende/phases/3/panels/3/di: Eighteen-year-old Rumi standing alone at the grave.
events/1225_larende/phases/3/panels/4/di: The funeral procession going out through the town gate.
His mother was buried at Larende. Seven hundred years later there is still a small mosque in Karaman that local people call the Mosque of Rumi's Mother.
events/1225_larende/phases/4/situation: The same desk, the same pen. This time what has to be written is an epitaph.
events/1225_larende/phases/4/question: If it were yours to write one line for his mother, you would write —
events/1225_larende/phases/4/options/0/t: 「She walked six years, carrying the house on her back.」
events/1225_larende/phases/4/options/1/t: 「She stopped here, and that is how we came to have a home.」
events/1225_larende/phases/4/options/2/t: 「In the driest stretch of the desert she gave me her water.」
events/1225_larende/phases/4/sameNote: No source records the line Rumi wrote. What you wrote is the answer to this one.
events/1225_larende/phases/4/diffNote: No source records the line Rumi wrote. What you wrote is the answer to this one.
events/1225_larende/phases/4/reveal:
There is no correct answer here.
About Mumina the reliable record says exactly one thing: she was buried at Larende.
events/1225_larende/phases/4/consequence: Two years later his father took his son north to Konya — the sultan was waiting for them.
events/1231_konya/phases/0/transitionTex: A mosque and a palace on the hill of Alaeddin, a wall around the whole of it. This is the capital of the Sultanate of Rum.
events/1231_konya/phases/0/announcement/: Sultan Kayqubad I invites Baha al-Din Walad to teach in the capital, Konya.
events/1231_konya/phases/0/narrative: Walad: 「My grandfather taught in Konya for only three years.」
events/1231_konya/phases/1/narrative:
A square inner courtyard, pointed arcades on all four sides, a pool of water in the middle. Blue-green glazed tile on the walls.
His father's chair has stood empty for seven days.
events/1231_konya/phases/1/instruction: Three people under the arcade. Talk to all of them.
events/1231_konya/phases/1/npcs/0/dialog: 「The old master could spend a whole afternoon on one sentence.」
「And now he is gone. Who teaches?」
events/1231_konya/phases/1/npcs/1/dialog: 「Law is something you spend a lifetime teaching. Can a man of twenty-four teach it?」
events/1231_konya/phases/1/npcs/2/dialog: 「I was your father's student. I came looking for him all the way from Balkh.」
「Nine years on the road. I arrived to find he had already gone.」
「Tomorrow you take the chair. I will sit below and listen.」
events/1231_konya/phases/2/situation:
On the morning he is to teach, he stands under the arcade staring at the wall.
Blue-green and black tiles make eight-pointed and ten-pointed stars, ring inside ring, with no visible place to begin.
events/1231_konya/phases/2/options/0/tex: Craftsmen laid it tile by tile, by eye
events/1231_konya/phases/2/options/1/tex: With compass and straightedge, worked out step by step from a single circle
events/1231_konya/phases/2/options/2/tex: Copied from the pattern of a carpet
events/1231_konya/phases/2/sameNote: Right. This wall was calculated, not drawn.
events/1231_konya/phases/2/diffNote: Not by eye, and not copied. —
events/1231_konya/phases/2/reveal:
Begin with one circle: divide it evenly, join the points, divide again. Every star and polygon follows from a handful of compass-and-straightedge rules.
Seljuk craftsmen learned geometry as a trade.
events/1231_konya/phases/2/consequence:
A pattern like this has no centre and no edge — start from any tile and it will tile outward forever.
The craftsmen used it to mean “infinite.”
Twenty-seven years from now, Rumi will stand in front of another wall and remember this.
events/1231_konya/phases/3/situation: His father is dead. The first time at the lectern, with his father's old students sitting below. Some of them are whispering.
events/1231_konya/phases/3/options/0/tex: The students scatter and find another master
events/1231_konya/phases/3/options/1/tex: He teaches well and they stay — but Burhan al-Din says one sentence to him
events/1231_konya/phases/3/options/2/tex: He declines, and asks Burhan al-Din to teach instead
events/1231_konya/phases/3/sameNote: Right. He held it — but the point of this one is the sentence that came after.
events/1231_konya/phases/3/diffNote: He held it. The real question comes after —
events/1231_konya/phases/3/reveal:
Burhan al-Din waited until the hall had emptied:
「What you have learned is your father's learning. But the thing your father tasted, you have not tasted yet.」
(The sense of it as reported by Sipahsalar and others, rewritten for this work.)
events/1231_konya/phases/3/consequence: So Burhan al-Din sent him to Syria — to read to the end of the books.
events/1233_syria/phases/0/travelNarrati: Burhan al-Din sees him out of the city. South over the Taurus mountains is Syria.
events/1233_syria/phases/0/instruction: Click each stop along the route.
events/1233_syria/phases/0/waypoints/0/d: 「Go and read. Read until there are no books left.」
events/1233_syria/phases/0/waypoints/2/d: Study at the Halawiyya madrasa. Law, commentary, grammar, logic.
events/1233_syria/phases/0/waypoints/3/d: More scholars live in this city than anywhere else in the world. The great Ibn Arabi is said to be here too.
Did they meet? There is no proof. Later books like to say so, but nobody alive at the time wrote it down.
events/1233_syria/phases/1/question: 「Go in. Forty days. You do not have to do anything.」
events/1233_syria/phases/1/options/0/reb: 「Open that door and the forty days start again from one.」
events/1233_syria/phases/1/options/1/tex: (A student has sent a letter from Konya. Open it.)
events/1233_syria/phases/1/options/1/reb: 「The letter is about what is outside. You are not outside.」
events/1233_syria/phases/1/options/2/tex: (The smell of cooking drifts in at the window.)
events/1233_syria/phases/1/options/2/reb: 「You are hungry. I know. That is one of the things to put down.」
events/1233_syria/phases/1/options/3/tex: (There is still a book inside your robe. Take it out and read.)
events/1233_syria/phases/1/options/3/reb: 「Reading too much is precisely why you are in here.」
events/1233_syria/phases/1/noise/1: (A cat jumps onto the window ledge.)
events/1233_syria/phases/1/noise/4: (What day is it? You have lost count.)
events/1233_syria/phases/1/silenceReveal:
Your hand stopped.
Nothing left in the room but an oil lamp and the shaft of light from the window, sliding slowly from the east wall to the west.
On the fortieth day the door opened.
events/1233_syria/phases/1/consequence:
Burhan al-Din said: 「Now you have in you the thing your father had.」
According to the later biographies he did this forty-day retreat three times.
events/1233_syria/phases/2/claim: The Rumi of 1240 is a scholar, and not yet a poet.
events/1233_syria/phases/2/instruction: Out of everything you have seen along the way, pick the 2 items that really support this.
events/1233_syria/phases/2/items/0/text: He spent years on law and scripture in Aleppo and Damascus, then taught in Konya to a full house.
events/1233_syria/phases/2/items/0/why: This is exactly what he is doing “now”: teaching, expounding. A scholar's life.
events/1233_syria/phases/2/items/1/text: What survives from him at this point is lecture and legal material, not poems.
events/1233_syria/phases/2/items/1/why: The hardest evidence for what someone is now is what they are leaving behind now.
events/1233_syria/phases/2/items/2/text: He went on to write tens of thousands of lines and became one of the greatest poets in Persian.
events/1233_syria/phases/2/items/2/why: True, but it belongs to later. You cannot use the future as evidence about the present — that is the real trap in this one.
events/1233_syria/phases/2/items/3/text: Damascus was one of the cities with the most scholars anywhere.
events/1233_syria/phases/2/items/3/why: True, but it is about the city, not about him.
events/1233_syria/phases/2/items/4/why: Retreat is a spiritual practice; scholars and poets alike do it. It cannot tell the two apart.
events/1233_syria/phases/2/closing:
Two are enough: what he is doing, and what he is leaving behind.
The tempting one is “he became a great poet” — but that is about the years after 1244.
Evidence has to line up with the time you are judging.
events/1233_syria/phases/3/narrative:
Walad: 「That year my father was thirty-three.
There was no longer a book he had not read.」
events/1244_shams/phases/0/transitionTex: The Mongols have come. This time it is not a rumour.
events/1244_shams/phases/0/announcement/:
The Seljuk army is beaten by the Mongols at Kösedăğ.
From now on the Sultanate of Rum is a Mongol vassal.
events/1244_shams/phases/0/narrative:
Walad: 「Everyone in the city was asking the same thing: is the world ending?
The next autumn, a stranger came through the gate.」
events/1244_shams/phases/1/narrative: Autumn 1244, Konya. A stranger has arrived in the city and taken a room at the sugar merchants' inn. Nobody knows who he is.
events/1244_shams/phases/1/instruction: People at the inn are talking about him. Hear two of them out.
events/1244_shams/phases/1/npcs/0/dialog: 「The man does not pay for his room.」
「And he swapped the good lock on his door for a broken one — he says a good lock is how you make people think there is treasure inside.」
events/1244_shams/phases/1/npcs/1/dialog: 「There is nothing in his room. A straw mat and a cracked jug.」
「But the things he asked me… I sell sugar. I had no answer for him.」
events/1244_shams/phases/1/npcs/2/dialog: 「The master rode down this street on his mule today.」
「Every scholar in the city dismounts to greet him. What do you suppose that odd man will make of it?」
events/1244_shams/phases/2/introBeats/0/: Rumi is thirty-seven, the most respected scholar in the city. He is sitting by the pool, reading. A ragged wandering dervish comes over and points at the books beside him.
events/1244_shams/phases/2/introBeats/2/: 「These are things you would not understand.」
events/1244_shams/phases/2/books/0/note: You saved your father's book. But the thing your father tasted will not fit inside a book — Burhan al-Din told him so years ago.
events/1244_shams/phases/2/books/1/note: You saved al-Mutanabbi — Rumi's favourite book. The story goes that Shams later forbade him to read it: stop reciting other men's poems and write your own.
events/1244_shams/phases/2/books/2/note: You saved the law book — thirteen years of teaching, and his living. What Shams is about to ask lies precisely outside these books.
events/1244_shams/phases/2/outroBeats/1/: 「This is something you would not understand.」
events/1244_shams/phases/2/noneNote: You did not reach for any of them — perhaps you had already guessed the books would be fine.
events/1244_shams/phases/2/reveal:
The same sentence, turned around.
A moment ago Rumi used it to fend off a stranger. Now it has landed back on Rumi.
events/1244_shams/phases/2/consequence:
This is a later legend, not documented fact (Aflaki wrote his Manaqib decades after Rumi's death), and the dialogue is rewritten for this work.
But the legend catches the weight of the meeting: a scholar who lived by books is asked, for the first time, about what lies outside them.
events/1244_shams/phases/3/legend: Legend · dialogue rewritten for this work
events/1244_shams/phases/3/question: 「You have read all these books — and you yourself, what do you know?」
events/1244_shams/phases/3/options/0/tex: 「I can recite every school's commentary on the classics, word for word.」
events/1244_shams/phases/3/options/0/reb: 「That is what the commentators know. I asked about you.」
events/1244_shams/phases/3/options/1/tex: 「My father Baha al-Din taught me: knowledge is the ladder to truth.」
events/1244_shams/phases/3/options/1/reb: 「That is your father's ladder. How many rungs have you climbed yourself?」
events/1244_shams/phases/3/options/2/tex: 「I have taught for thirteen years. The whole city comes to hear me.」
events/1244_shams/phases/3/options/2/reb: 「They come to hear you recite. Has anyone ever heard your own voice?」
events/1244_shams/phases/3/silenceReveal:
You did not answer.
Shams smiled: 「That is the truest thing you have said today.」
events/1244_shams/phases/3/consequence:
For months afterwards Rumi turned away almost all his students and spent his days behind a closed door with Shams. The students were jealous and furious.
And this scholar, who had spent a lifetime expounding scripture, began writing poems — the enormous lyric collection he left (more than three thousand ghazals) is signed not with his own name but with the name of Shams.
events/1244_shams/phases/3/noise/2: 「In the third volume of the commentary it is written…」
events/1244_shams/phases/3/noise/3: 「There is a line in my father's Ma'arif…」
events/1244_shams/phases/4/situation:
Over the next three years Rumi wrote a thousand lyric poems.
Persian lyric has a rule: the closing couplet carries the poet's own pen name.
events/1244_shams/phases/4/question: Whose name is in the closing couplet of Rumi's poems?
events/1244_shams/phases/4/sameNote: You had it. Then you already understand what that meeting turned him into.
events/1244_shams/phases/4/reveal:
He called the whole collection the Divan of Shams.
In the place where his own name belonged, he put the name of the man who stopped him.
events/1244_shams/phases/4/consequence:
A scholar spends a lifetime learning to sign his name.
Then he gives the place away.
events/1247_damascus/phases/0/claim: Shams left Konya in 1246 mainly because the people around Rumi could not tolerate him.
events/1247_damascus/phases/0/instructio: Out of these statements, pick the 2 that really support it.
events/1247_damascus/phases/0/items/0/te: The students complained: the master shuts himself in all day with a wanderer nobody can account for, and has stopped teaching.
events/1247_damascus/phases/0/items/0/wh: The plainest form of “could not tolerate”: he took their teacher away from them.
events/1247_damascus/phases/0/items/1/te: Some abused Shams to his face; others said openly that he would be dealt with.
events/1247_damascus/phases/0/items/1/wh: From complaint to threat — this is the hardest evidence of intolerance there is.
events/1247_damascus/phases/0/items/2/te: Shams came from Tabriz and was older than Rumi.
events/1247_damascus/phases/0/items/2/wh: True, and irrelevant to why he left.
events/1247_damascus/phases/0/items/3/te: Shams was in any case a wanderer who never stayed anywhere for long.
events/1247_damascus/phases/0/items/3/wh:
This one cuts against the claim: his leaving may have been nothing but his own habit.
Good judgement recognises the facts that count against it.
events/1247_damascus/phases/0/items/4/te: In 1247 Rumi's son Sultan Walad went to Damascus himself and brought him back.
events/1247_damascus/phases/0/items/4/wh: That is about bringing him back, not about why he left.
events/1247_damascus/phases/0/closing:
Complaint plus threat — those two stand up.
But do not forget the one that cuts against you: he was a man who never stayed.
The sources let us say “mainly because.” They do not let us say “only because.”
events/1247_damascus/phases/1/travelNarr:
He has disappeared a second time. This time Rumi goes himself.
The same road he took fourteen years ago — that time, to study.
events/1247_damascus/phases/1/instructio: Click each stop along the route.
events/1247_damascus/phases/1/waypoints/: 「Last time Walad went to fetch him. This time I go myself.」
The pass in winter. Snow to the horses' knees.
Asking all the way down. Nobody has seen a man in a black felt cap.
Arrived. Dark already. Half the bazaar is still open.
events/1247_damascus/phases/2/situation: The Damascus bazaar at night. A long arcade, shop after shop shuttered. Standing water on the ground catches what light there is.
events/1247_damascus/phases/2/instructio: You are carrying a lamp. Look for leads in the bazaar.
events/1247_damascus/phases/2/spots/0/cl: 「A man in a black felt cap? I think I saw him a few days ago… he went towards the north gate.」
events/1247_damascus/phases/2/spots/1/cl: 「He sat here one whole night. He was gone by daybreak.」
events/1247_damascus/phases/2/spots/2/cl: 「Shams? Never heard of him. Which man from Tabriz do you mean?」
events/1247_damascus/phases/2/spots/3/cl: 「Thousands come and go every day. Who remembers one stranger?」
events/1247_damascus/phases/2/options/0/: Jealous men killed him and threw the body down a well
events/1247_damascus/phases/2/options/1/: He went back to Tabriz and died there in old age
events/1247_damascus/phases/2/options/2/: He went somewhere further off and never turned back
events/1247_damascus/phases/2/options/3/: The sources have no answer — nobody knows
events/1247_damascus/phases/2/sameNote: You chose “nobody knows.” In history that is a real answer, and often the most honest one.
events/1247_damascus/phases/2/diffNote: You followed all four leads and all four came to nothing. What does that tell you?
events/1247_damascus/phases/2/reveal:
People have written down each of these versions.
The murder story comes from very late sources and no reliable evidence supports it; both Khoy in Iran and Konya in Turkey have a grave said to be his.
The reliable record tells us one thing only: after 1247, no one saw him again.
events/1247_damascus/phases/2/consequenc:
Rumi went to Damascus to look for him twice and never found him.
After the second journey home, he stopped looking.
events/1247_damascus/phases/3/situation:
Twenty-seven years ago an old man in a spice shop told him about a flock of birds.
Now he is carrying a lamp through an empty bazaar, looking for a man.
events/1247_damascus/phases/3/question: What did each search actually find? Link left to right.
events/1247_damascus/phases/3/left/0/tex: Flew over seven valleys to find their king
events/1247_damascus/phases/3/left/1/tex: Walked a whole city to find the man who stopped him
events/1247_damascus/phases/3/right/0/su: the reflection on the lake · the words coming out of his own mouth
events/1247_damascus/phases/3/right/2/te: Found nothing, and went home empty-handed
events/1247_damascus/phases/3/sameNote:
You ran both lines to the same place.
— That story, twenty-seven years ago, was a trailer for tonight.
events/1247_damascus/phases/3/diffNote: Look at the actual two lines: they land in the same place.
events/1247_damascus/phases/3/reveal:
What Rumi later wrote comes to something like this:
「Why am I still searching? He and I are the same.
His words are coming out of my own mouth.」
(Summarised for this work; not a word-for-word quotation.)
events/1247_damascus/phases/3/consequenc:
From here he stops writing about searching and starts writing about becoming.
Three years from now he will stop in the street of the goldsmiths.
events/1250_goldsmith/phases/0/narrative:
The goldsmiths' street in the Konya bazaar. A row of open shopfronts; forge fire, anvils, gold leaf catching the sun.
The whole street is ringing.
events/1250_goldsmith/phases/0/instructi: Three people in the street. Talk to all of them.
events/1250_goldsmith/phases/0/npcs/0/di: 「I cannot read. All I can do is beat metal.」
「The master says that when I strike, he can hear something else in it.」
events/1250_goldsmith/phases/0/npcs/1/di: 「Beating gold leaf takes a whole day for one piece — until the light goes through it.」
「Strike too hard and it tears. It has to be blow after blow, every one the same weight.」
events/1250_goldsmith/phases/0/npcs/2/di: 「The master is mixing with a metal-beater now.」
「Last time it was a wanderer, this time a man who cannot read. What does that make us?」
events/1250_goldsmith/phases/1/situation:
Forge light fills the shop. A sheet of gold on the anvil, the hammer coming down again and again, each blow a fixed weight.
Rumi stands in the street listening. What he hears is not metalwork — it is the bone of a line of verse.
events/1250_goldsmith/phases/1/question: Three ways of striking. Which line does each one beat out? Link left to right. (◼ long / ◻ short)
events/1250_goldsmith/phases/1/right/0/s: the ramal metre · all twenty-five thousand couplets
events/1250_goldsmith/phases/1/right/1/t: A beginner practising, aiming only for even weight
events/1250_goldsmith/phases/1/sameNote: You got the first line right.
events/1250_goldsmith/phases/1/diffNote: Here are the actual links — the first row is the one that matters.
events/1250_goldsmith/phases/1/reveal:
“long short long long ｜ long short long long ｜ long short long.”
That is the ramal metre. All twenty-five thousand couplets of the Masnavi run on it.
What you just linked is that book's heartbeat.
events/1250_goldsmith/phases/1/consequen:
The story goes that Rumi passed the goldsmith's shop, heard the hammering, and began to turn in the street.
Not a dance — a man finally catching a rhythm.
events/1250_goldsmith/phases/2/situation: The students are jealous again. Last time this happened, the man left and never came back.
events/1250_goldsmith/phases/2/question: What does Rumi do this time?
events/1250_goldsmith/phases/2/options/0: The same as with Shams — lets him go
events/1250_goldsmith/phases/2/options/1: Marries his son Sultan Walad to the goldsmith's daughter
events/1250_goldsmith/phases/2/sameNote: Right. He had learned — this time he locked the man inside his own family.
events/1250_goldsmith/phases/2/diffNote: He did not let anyone be driven off again. —
events/1250_goldsmith/phases/2/reveal:
He married his son to the goldsmith's daughter.
An illiterate craftsman became the in-law of a family of scholars.
events/1250_goldsmith/phases/2/consequen:
Salah al-Din stayed with Rumi for nearly ten years and died in 1258. Rumi wrote an elegy for him.
This time, nobody was driven away.
events/1258_masnavi/title: Song of the Reed · The Shelf of Parables
events/1258_masnavi/phases/0/transitionT: On the far horizon, a city is smoking.
events/1258_masnavi/phases/0/announcemen:
The Mongol army takes Baghdad. The Abbasid caliphate falls.
The same year, the goldsmith Salah al-Din dies.
events/1258_masnavi/phases/0/narrative: Walad: 「The world was collapsing. My father began dictating a long poem.」
events/1258_masnavi/phases/1/poemContext:
Husam al-Din is waiting with pen and paper. Rumi begins — put the words back where they belong.
(Based on Nicholson's English; rendered afresh for this work.)
events/1258_masnavi/phases/1/puzzle:
Listen to this reed: it is ___;
what it tells of is ___.
「Ever since I was cut from the ___,
my lament has made men and women weep.」
events/1258_masnavi/phases/1/narrative:
The reed was cut out of the reed bed, and has been crying ever since.
— In which of these chapters were you also taken away from home?
events/1258_masnavi/phases/2/situation: Four travelling companions — a Persian, an Arab, a Turk and a Greek — are given a single silver coin along the road. All four want to spend it on something to eat, each shouting for his own, and it is close to blows. You are standing at the fruit stall.
events/1258_masnavi/phases/2/goal: One silver coin buys one thing. Satisfy all four of them.
events/1258_masnavi/phases/2/travelers/0: 「angūr! The thing that grows on the vine!」
events/1258_masnavi/phases/2/travelers/2: 「üzüm! Purple, and sweeter still when it is dried!」
events/1258_masnavi/phases/2/travelers/3: 「istāfīl! The one you make wine from!」
events/1258_masnavi/phases/2/vendorLine: Stallholder: 「One silver coin buys one thing.」
events/1258_masnavi/phases/2/hint: …could all four of them be shouting for the same thing?
events/1258_masnavi/phases/2/reveal:
angūr, ʻinab, üzüm, istāfīl — four words, all of them “grapes.”
They wanted the same bunch of grapes, in four different languages.
events/1258_masnavi/phases/2/consequence:
In Book II of the Masnavi Rumi says: had there been one man there who knew many languages, he would have reconciled all four — with that single coin, buying the thing every one of them wanted.
Rumi lived in exactly such a city. Thirteenth-century Konya spoke Persian, Arabic, Turkish and Greek in the same street; he wrote in Persian, and left lines with Turkish and Greek mixed into them.
events/1258_masnavi/phases/3/situation: Someone has brought a thing from India and shut it in a pitch-dark room for people to see. There is no lamp; whoever goes in can only feel with their hands.
events/1258_masnavi/phases/3/instruction: All you have is one candle. Move the light, and feel.
events/1258_masnavi/phases/3/spots/0/cla: 「This thing is like a water pipe.」
events/1258_masnavi/phases/3/spots/2/cla: 「You are both wrong, it is like a pillar.」
events/1258_masnavi/phases/3/question: Four men say it is like a pipe, a fan, a pillar, a throne. What is actually in the dark room?
events/1258_masnavi/phases/3/options/0/t: Four different things — a pipe, a fan, a pillar and a throne are all in there
events/1258_masnavi/phases/3/options/1/t: One thing, too big for any one person to feel all of
events/1258_masnavi/phases/3/options/2/t: A storeroom full of junk, with everything in it
events/1258_masnavi/phases/3/sameNote: You assembled four partial reports into one whole.
events/1258_masnavi/phases/3/diffNote: All four were telling the truth — each had felt only one piece.
events/1258_masnavi/phases/3/reveal:
It is an elephant.
「If each of them had held a candle, their accounts would not have differed.」
— Masnavi, Book III (rendered for this work)
events/1258_masnavi/phases/3/consequence:
Now look at yourself: your candle also lit only a small circle, exactly like theirs. You guessed the whole by setting several accounts side by side.
The story is far older than Rumi: the blind men and the elephant appear in Buddhist scripture (the Dīrgha Āgama among others), and the Persian poet Sana'i told it before him. Rumi's change was to make them sighted men in a dark room — what stops them is not their eyes, it is the lack of light.
events/1258_masnavi/phases/4/situation:
The sultan sets Chinese painters against Greek painters to see who has the greater art. Two rooms face each other with a curtain hung between them.
The Chinese painters ask the sultan for a hundred pigments and paint every day; the Greek painters ask for no pigment at all, shut their door, and do one thing only —
events/1258_masnavi/phases/4/instruction: You are the Greek painter. Hold and rub the wall until it shines.
events/1258_masnavi/phases/4/polishedNot: The wall is polished bright as water — and right now all it reflects is the curtain opposite.
events/1258_masnavi/phases/4/question: The day of the contest, the curtain is about to be drawn. What do you think happens?
events/1258_masnavi/phases/4/options/0/t: The Greeks lose — there is nothing painted on their wall
events/1258_masnavi/phases/4/options/1/t: The polished wall reflects the whole painting opposite, brighter in the light than the original
events/1258_masnavi/phases/4/options/2/t: The sultan finds them equal and calls it a draw
events/1258_masnavi/phases/4/sameNote: You saw what the mirror was for.
events/1258_masnavi/phases/4/diffNote: The Greek painters were betting on something else —
events/1258_masnavi/phases/4/reveal:
The sultan looks first at the Chinese wall and is entranced; then he turns to the Greek wall — the whole painting opposite is inside it, moving as the light moves.
Rumi says: the Greek painters are like those on the path. They do not pile up learning; they only polish the heart until it can reflect everything.
— Masnavi, Book I (summarised for this work)
events/1258_masnavi/phases/4/consequence:
But do not forget: the painting in the mirror was made stroke by stroke by the Chinese painters. Without the wall opposite, the mirror reflects nothing.
In Persian poetry “the Chinese painter” is already shorthand for surpassing skill — and Rumi has a wall with nothing on it beat exactly that.
One more small secret: “Greek” in Persian is “Rūmī,” meaning the lands of Anatolia — which is where the name Rumi itself comes from.
events/1258_masnavi/phases/5/transitionT: The old man speaks with his eyes closed against the cushions; the young man bends over the low desk writing fast. The floor is covered with finished sheets.
events/1258_masnavi/phases/5/announcemen:
Six books, some twenty-five thousand couplets.
The sixth was never finished — the last story breaks off halfway, and the poet died.
events/1273_wedding/phases/0/transitionT: 1273 年冬，科尼亚。雪落在屋顶上。
events/1273_wedding/phases/0/announcemen:
父亲病了。他对我们说：
「不要哭。这是我的婚礼。」
events/1273_wedding/phases/1/legend: 台词为本作改写 · 送葬场面据阿夫拉基《圣徒传》
events/1273_wedding/phases/1/situation: 1273 年冬，科尼亚。鲁米病了。他对身边的人说：不要哭，这是我的婚礼。病榻前摆着几样东西——每一样，都是一路上有人给他的。
events/1273_wedding/phases/1/people/0/li: 「这孩子将来，会在世上点起一把火。」
events/1273_wedding/phases/1/people/1/li: 「现在你身上，有了你父亲的那样东西。」
events/1273_wedding/phases/1/walkPrompt: 1273 年 12 月 17 日，鲁米去世。第二天清晨，送葬的队伍出发了。
events/1273_wedding/phases/1/question: 送葬的队伍里，有基督徒，也有犹太人。他们为什么也来了？
events/1273_wedding/phases/1/options/0/t: 苏丹下令，全城的人都要来
events/1273_wedding/phases/1/options/1/t: 他们觉得，鲁米也是自己的老师
events/1273_wedding/phases/1/reveal: 据阿夫拉基记载，有人问他们为何而来，他们大意是说：「我们从他身上，懂得了我们自己经书里的道理。」
events/1273_wedding/phases/1/consequence:
科尼亚当时住着突厥人、波斯人、希腊人、亚美尼亚人和犹太人——就像那四个争葡萄的旅伴，说着不同的话。鲁米讲的寓言，谁都听得懂。
鲁米管自己的死叫「婚礼之夜」。七百多年后，每年 12 月 17 日，科尼亚还在纪念这一夜。
同一年，远在东方，襄阳在蒙古大军的围困中陷落。
events/1273_wedding/phases/2/instruction: 点击画面，一格一格看下去。
events/1273_wedding/phases/2/panels/0/di: 「他握着我的手，像要把什么交给我。」
events/1273_wedding/phases/2/panels/1/di: 送葬的队伍里，不同衣着的人并肩走着。
events/1273_wedding/phases/2/panels/2/di: 后来，墓上建起一座绿色的穹顶。
events/1273_wedding/phases/2/panels/3/di: 每年 12 月 17 日，科尼亚都会举行纪念。七百多年了，人们还叫它「婚礼之夜」。

鲁米去世的 1273 年，襄阳在蒙古大军的围困中陷落；三年后，南宋的都城临安也降了。
当年逼得鲁米一家背井离乡的那支铁骑，此时正在中国的土地上。
